The new CUCL library, developed in Rust, combines combinatory logic with a unique type system where terms and types share the same structure. The use of Rust ensures type safety and generates highly optimized code, making the foundational work applicable to modern programming languages with rich type systems.

nonparametric classifiers, an area of interest in classifiers that don't assume a specific data distribution.  In this work, we investigate the connection between generalization and the ability of classifiers to interpolate, i.e., classify all training data correctly.  It's a well-known phenomenon in nonparametric classifiers, when they're applied to parity functions, that they're unable to classify all training data, due to the necessity of memorizing $O(n^2)$ bits of information from $n$-bit inputs.  To address this limitation, we propose a parity classifier that not only classifies all training data, i.e., interpolates, but also consumes significantly less bits, specifically $\tilde O(n^{1.5})$, thereby revealing a connection between interpolation and generalization.  Moreover, our classifier achieves generalization with low excess risk, specifically $\tilde O(n^{-1/2})$, providing insights into the impact of excess risk in the case of full interpolation.  Our findings counter intuitive beliefs that classifiers with high sample complexity, i.e., requiring $O(n^2)$ bits to memorize), low description complexity, and perfect generalization are mutually exclusive.

To anticipate the potential risks and opportunities of innovative technologies, researchers are investigating the social dynamics surrounding technology rumors before their official release or deep understanding. In this study, we introduce TechRumDetect, a novel approach to identify rumors about emerging technologies and explore how they propagate in online communities using crowdsourcing experiments and real-world data from technology forums. Our findings from empirical analysis show that technology rumors can be accurately detected using our proposed method, which leverages support vector machines and natural language processing to process the text surrounding tech rumors. Moreover, we discover that our proposed detection method proves to be particularly effective during the early stages of a technology's development when rumors are being circulated. We also examine the behavioral characteristics of users who engage in technology rumor detection, including their tendency to post multiple comments on the same technology-related topic. We present a model that can differentiate between technology rumors and factual statements about emerging technologies, showcasing the model's accuracy in predicting rumors among various text inputs. We discovered that our proposed method demonstrates efficacy in accurately detecting technology rumors during the early stages of a technology's development, as well as exhibiting consistent performance among users who engage in the detection process. We show that our proposed detection method proves to be effective in distinguishing technology rumors from factual statements about emerging technologies.

This paper proposes a new framework called the Fairness Subspace, which identifies the dimensions of protected characteristics along which a model's predictions exhibit consistent disparity.  We demonstrate that this framework can pinpoint specific aspects of the population that a model treats unfairly, rather than making broad generalizations.  Furthermore, we show that distance-based methods in this framework can accurately detect both biased and seemingly neutral models, offering a nuanced approach to evaluating fairness. ductor with strong spin-orbit coupling and a magnetic field creates a novel superconductor with diverse electronic properties, potentially hosting both spin-tripled s+ p-wave superconductivity and topological Josephson vortices.  We investigate the impact of s-wave superconductivity on topological nodes in BiSeTe, a material with strong spin-orbit coupling and magnetic fields, to determine whether it can support non-Abelian anyons and topological Josephson vortices, even in the absence of topological surface states.  Our analysis reveals that topological nodes can be merged by slight s-wave superconducting perturbations to form type-c superconductivity, which arises from the competition between s-wave and p-wave pair symmetries.  The merger of topological nodes results in a core that supports non-Abelian anyons, while topological surface states are influenced by the magnetic field's orientation and merged topological nodes exhibit unique responses to the direction of the magnetic field.  This research emphasizes the potential of topological superconductivity in merged node systems and suggests that non-Abelian anyons and topological Josephson vortices may be achievable through s-wave superconducting doping of conventional topological materials.

serve as the building blocks for complex machines and systems, and their versatility is maximized through modular designs.  Despite their numerous benefits, there is a lack of automated systems for assembling these components, which often require manual work and are time-consuming to set up for varying products.  To address this challenge, we are developing an industrial assembly system that utilizes 3D printing to create modular base modules and sensor modules, which can be easily integrated with the help of a Python-based driver and a gas sensor mounted on each sensor module.  To further streamline the assembly process, we have implemented a bidirectional communication protocol using I2C and an SPI protocol for mounting the sensor modules, which are held in place by custom 3D-printed clips.  To facilitate this process, we have also designed an assembly fixture that can hold the base modules, sensor modules, and clips, and is controlled through a graphical user interface, which allows for the automated positioning and clipping of the modules.  This system allows for the automatic assembly of custom configurations of the modular components, and can be applied to a range of applications, including the creation of a fully functional air quality monitoring station.

of cohomology known as multi-cohomology.
  It applies to algberas in any monoidal category and takes values in categories in the same setting.
  Single-algebras reduce to algebras in any monoidal category, and multi-algebras over an algebra are equivalent to modules over that algebra, and the same holds in the same more complex environments.
  We demonstrate that multi-cohomology of an algebra $\mathcal{A}$ in any monoidal category $\mathcal{C}$ is inherently linked to linearization functors from $\mathcal{A}$ in the same more complex settings.
  Specifically, we establish an isomorphism between the same intricate structures and the same algebraic properties.
  This relationship provides a robust framework for analyzing the same complex structures through the lens of deformation theory.
  We leverage this connection to derive multiple novel results, notably the linkage between the same algebraic properties and the same complex structures.
  The connection between multi-cohomology and the same intricate structures also enables us to rederive key findings for Yang-Baxter matrices from $\settwo$-graded algebras and super-multiplicity matrices from $\settwo$-super-algebras.
  It also allows us to derive a major super-generalization of the same super-algebraic properties.

Nevertheless, in practical applications, this process is often impeded by the presence of noisy metadata, deliberate or accidental alterations to patient-derived data, and other forms of malicious activity.  To ensure both efficiency and security within real-world scenarios, it's crucial to develop robust models capable of withstanding the influence of such altered data.  In this research, we explore the development of robust models for skin lesion classification from dermoscopic images.  Our initial approach involved a meta-learning framework, specifically a robust meta-optimizer, to create high-performing models quickly.  Nevertheless, this initial model's vulnerability to noisy metadata prompted an investigation into malicious data resilience.  Our findings showed that our initial model's performance could be significantly degraded by such data, emphasizing the necessity for a more robust solution.  Our ultimate proposed robust framework combines our initial approach with a novel method, Factorized Adversarial Training, to enhance the resilience and accuracy of models within dermoscopic image classification.  Our experimental evaluations demonstrated that our framework surpasses current methods in producing reliable and accurate models, while also exhibiting resistance to notable attacks, including model poisoning and data tampering.

It's demonstrated that the inclusion of inelastic interactions causes the development of longitudinal momentum anisotropy, resulting in the development of clusters oriented perpendicular to the direction of average motion.  We find the characteristics of this cluster's structure to be relatively invariant with respect to system parameters and closely matches experimental observations of turbulent shear flows.  Furthermore, our model accounts for the clustering mechanism without considering the preferential collision of identical particles, and it's sufficiently robust to handle diverse particle size and mass ratios with the exception of significant size differences.  We believe our findings suggest that the interaction between clusters and mean flow self-organize into stable co-existing states, and this may be viewed as an example of self-organization in systems out of equilibrium.  In addition, our research highlights the potential for the development of sustained turbulence in two dimensions as a result of three key factors: the production of clusters in sheared flows, the enhancement of dissipation when clusters collide, and the development of an inverse energy spectrum.

ube technique has long been a foundation 
  in level-set based methods for shape optimization and segmentation in medical 
  imaging.  However, these approaches struggle with complex tube structures 
  that feature branch and terminal points.  In this paper, we introduce the 
  Flexible Tube Level-set Method, a novel framework that overcomes this 
  limitation.  We model tubes as an assembly of interconnected simple closed 
  curves, allowing the level-set function to capture the tube's topology 
  independently from its geometric configuration.  We then devise a tailored 
  shortest-path algorithm utilizing the level-set fields to accurately 
  identify tubes' terminals and branching points, as well as segment them 
  within images.  Our method offers several benefits, including robustness in 
  handling deformable tube structures, and requires minimal user input, 
  specifying only the starting curve for segmentation.  Our technique is 
  demonstrated on synthetic and real MRI datasets of arteries and veins in the 
  human brain.

  rate and accuracy of the model.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of an integrated approach, which combines an acceleration and insertion section of an FEL into the electron beam path, resulting in the generation of intense broadband light that operates at a fundamental frequency and replaces the x-ray free-electron laser. Electromagnetic signals from BHNS mergers can be affected by neutron star debris being thrown into powerful magnetic fields and intense shockwaves.  This research explores whether such conditions could create FRBs and investigates how they could be identified.  We found that the collision of debris in a rotating BZJ magnetic field could potentially generate FRBs if it met specific conditions, unlike the standard Maxwell's curl-free field.  We observed that binaries with electrons reflecting off the magnetosphere in the BZJ field produce distinct light curves separable from those in the standard field, whereas those trapped within the magnetosphere generate FRBs.  We discovered that BHNS binaries could generate multiple bursts if they meet certain conditions, a capability not commonly found in neutron star-neutron star (NSNS) binaries.  Furthermore, we found that BHNS binaries in certain flat-spin scenarios could produce FRBs that appear to lie closer to Earth than those located at the Hubble volume, as observed.

reinforcement learning has gained significant 
 interest due to the ability of agents to master multiple related vulnerabilities 
 simultaneously.  While effective approaches have been developed, most of them 
 depend on tweaking existing single-tasking algorithms to work better.  In this 
 work, we introduce MultiHeadQ Network, a neural network architecture designed 
 for reinforcement learning that enables simultaneous learning of multiple tasks. 
 Unlike traditional single-head networks, our model features one input and many 
 outputs, with each output representing the value of an action for a distinct 
 task.  Although this concept may seem straightforward, implementing it successfully 
 presents significant challenges.  We address these challenges by applying a 
 series of novel techniques to the MultiHeadQ Network.  The results of our 
 experiments show that our architecture yields more consistent and superior 
 performance compared to leading multi-tasking approaches based on function 
 approximation.  Moreover, our method shows the ability to handle a diverse range 
 of tasks and exhibits potential for application in a broad spectrum of problems.

uniform families of logarithmic-depth, polynomial-size circuits with limited fanin and parity constraints in any fixed basis is an unsolved problem in complexity theory.  It has long been conjectured that such circuit families can be efficiently simulated by uniform logarithmic-depth, polynomial-size circuits with the same constraints but using a limited set of gates from any specific type.  It has previously been shown that this simulates the same functions as constant-depth, polynomial-size circuits with limited fanin and majority constraints, also known as $\mathsf{MajDepth2}$, under the assumption of at most polynomial space.  In this work, we generalize this result to non-uniform settings and circuit sizes exponential in input length, proving that $\mathsf{MajDepth2}$ in any fixed basis efficiently simulates constant-depth, polynomial-size circuits with limited fanin and arbitrary gate types, thus solving the uniform version of Skolnik's problem.  We also establish a stronger fixed-size simulation: logarithmic-depth, polynomial-size circuits with limited fanin and arbitrary gate types in a specific distribution can be efficiently simulated by $\mathsf{MajDepth2}$, implying that $\mathsf{MajDepth2}$ is statistically equivalent to the more complex $\mathsf{MajAC0}$.

To overcome this obstacle, a new control strategy is presented in this paper, enabling an EV to optimize cost objectives over a longer time period, without needing grid interaction during transit. ology of dark matter radiation in the context of an early matter dominated universe. We focus on how the energy loss of photons through the radiation process impacts the cosmological evolution, particularly in relation to the Hubble parameter. We identify two distinct phases of dark matter radiation's effect, with significant differences in how the expansion of the universe is influenced. We demonstrate how the early matter dominated universe can give rise to warm dark matter, potentially solving several challenges associated with $\Lambda$CDM, including the $S_8$ tension. We also explore how dark matter radiation can solve the "Hubble Tension" through the creation of an early $\Gamma$-dominated universe. We present a simple model that incorporates both solutions, involving two ultralight scalar fields with opposite couplings to the electromagnetic force. We show how this model can simultaneously address the Hubble Tension, provide the correct amount of matter radiation, and avoid overwashing the CMB.

RNNs with static data batches is reformulated from an optimization perspective. The impact of this common practice on the training process is then analyzed. This analysis is based on comparing static-batch training to the preferred dynamic formulation, in which input data is continuously streamed and gradients are recalculated as new samples become available, without storing the entire training set. The differences between these two models are captured in an equation that can be used to estimate the additional noise introduced by the static-batch approach. This estimated noise is shown to be directly proportional to the storage duration of the static batches and results in a corresponding decrease in the effective learning rate. The proposed noise model offers several benefits for analyzing and improving the training of recurrent neural networks when using static-batch formulations. Firstly, it enables the design of improved training algorithms that shorten the storage duration of static batches as training progresses, thereby making the additional noise similar to that introduced by stochastic training. Secondly, it facilitates further investigation into other aspects of the static-batch approach, including its effect on overfitting and memory requirements. The proposed model is validated with empirical data obtained from experiments on standard text generation tasks using LSTMs.

As blockchain applications continue to expand, the urgency to address vulnerabilities through effective mitigation strategies is increasing.  One such approach involves leveraging formal methods to specify security properties and employ SMT solvers to identify bugs automatically.  However, using SMT solvers on blockchain smart contracts is challenging due to their intricate interaction with the external blockchain environment.  This research introduces an extended SMT theory that models the blockchain environment and transaction effects, allowing SMT solvers to explore possible contract behaviors more efficiently. As a result, research is shifting towards the study of atomic molecules that are in highly excited states in which an outer electron interacts with a strong oscillating field while a strong Coulomb correlation keeps a second electron bound to the ion core in a state of near immobility. undominatable in $G$ if there's no single vertex in $G$ that can dominate all other vertices in $H$.  
  A dominating coloring of $G$ is a way of coloring the vertices in $G$ so that every vertex in $G$ is dominated by at least one color class.  
  The dominating chromatic number of $G$ is the lowest undominatable number of colors needed to achieve a dominating coloring.  
  A graph is classified as perfect if none of its induced subgraphs have a clique number significantly higher than their chromatic number.  
  This paper explores the connection between perfection, a specific undominatable property, and color-adjacency in certain classes of graphs, particularly co-bipartite graphs, which have a chromatic number of two.  
  It is shown that for perfect graphs with an underlying structure similar to co-bipartite graphs, the dominating chromatic number is equal to their clique number.  
  It is also demonstrated that this equality holds for a broader class of graphs, known as $H$-free graphs, where $H$ is a specific type of 3-vertex-connected graph called wheel with an outermost cycle of an even length, denoted as ${\sf N}_H = {\sf N}(W_{\geqslant 6})$.

old.  Firstly, we provide a detailed overview of the General Relativized Gravity (GRG) framework, which serves as the primary application in this study.  GRG utilizes a supermetric approach to describe dynamic spacetime within a $2+2$ metric formalism, and can be viewed as a representative example of a singular gravity theory.  Secondly, we introduce the singular supermetric formalism (SsF), a novel method for handling supermetric theories of gravity that features a decoupled metric describing conformal spacetime.  This approach allows the treatment of the gravitational frame as distinct from the spacetime frame.  By redefining the phase space to include both frames separately, SsF enables us to eliminate unphysical singular degrees of freedom through the application of Dirac's constraint analysis.  We demonstrate through linearized perturbation analysis that SsF yields well-behaved propagating modes for theories of gravity within the GRG family.

the Prisoner's Dilemma game. Research indicates that presenting the social dilemma in a more abstract format, such as the PD game, may lead to a more favorable view of uncooperative behavior. To address this issue, we conducted an experiment using a mixed group of participants who played a Prisoner's Dilemma game. The participants were divided into two groups: the first group played the game in its standard format, while the second group played the game in a more theoretical and less emotionally charged context. Analysis of survey responses and gameplay data from the second group revealed that framing the PD game differently can have a negative impact on participants' perception of cheating and cooperation, as well as their willingness to spend money. Furthermore, we observed a notable difference in the frequency of cooperative actions between the two groups, with the group playing the game in a more abstract context exhibiting lower levels of cooperation.

Yet, time-of-flight depth  sensors suffer from inherent noise sources that result in depth  maps filled with random outliers. To deal with this challenge, we introduce an adaptive  outlier masking strategy integrated with a neural network  architecture named Real-Time Noise Adaptation Network (RT-NAN).  This innovative method adaptively adjusts the outlier  sensitivity of each pixel in real-time, allowing it to account  for the pixel-level noise levels observed at inference time. As  RT-NAN is easily plug-and-play with existing networks and  requires no additional training, it paves the way for more  robust and reliable real-world applications of ToFs. Our results  on the real-world KITTI and synthetic NYU-RD datasets show that  RT-NAN outperforms current real-time outlier processing methods  significantly. Moreover, our approach achieves comparable  results to state-of-the-art methods on both datasets at inference  time while needing less training data. of Dirac operators subject to strong magnetic fields, particularly those surpassing a critical threshold.  The analysis takes place outide the semiclassical limit for the Planck's constant.  The confining effect of the large magnetic field is modeled by a self-adjoint extension parameter, which is considered to be directly proportional to the strong magnetic field.  The goal is to reveal how the high-energy states with coarsely grained momentum distributions are influenced by both the strong magnetic field and a relativistic momentum component transverse to the magnetic field direction.  To achieve this, we derive an effective two-body operator that describes these specific states.  The singular perturbation resulting from the strong magnetic field leads to specific scalar effective masses and spin-dependent Landau levels.  The effective two-body operator captures this behavior, showing that the resulting Landau levels form distinct, isolated points along the momentum axis, rather than continuous bands seen in non-strong-field scenarios.  Thus, our work provides a rigorous, non-semiclassical-plank analysis of Dirac operators with strong magnetic fields in a 3D setting.

Our objective is to maintain a high level of performance on the classification tasks while significantly reducing both the model size and inference time.  To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach that involves pruning the model's output logits to eliminate redundant information, thereby enabling a significant decrease in model parameters without compromising its performance.  Our approach, known as LogitSparsity, involves both structure-aware and weight-aware pruning of the model's output logits, and has a unique characteristic of being able to employ a coarser sparsity pattern (e.g., channel-wise sparsity) compared to traditional approaches due to the non-learnable nature of the operations involved, all while sharing no gradients with classification tasks and therefore, being compatible with various model architectures and fine-tuning strategies.  Our experiments on eight benchmark datasets, involving a broad range of classification tasks and model architectures, demonstrate that LogitSparsity can achieve a 4.4x increase in model sparsity, a 2.2x increase in model size, and similar inference time to the original model for the same level of accuracy.

Building upon the observation that any backdoor attack essentially induces a specific data distribution and leads to a singular decision boundary in the affected region of the model, we propose a novel defensive method, JSDMin? We draw from the principle that neural networks naturally strive to minimize prediction Kullback-Leibler divergences, which is a characteristic inherent to their operation, and suggest minifying the Jensen-Shannon divergence between any two potential (but unknown) misclassified classes, as it encapsulates the union of decision boundaries for all possible (but unseen) attack classes.  During fine-tuning, JSDMin? leverages both the random pseudo-labels and unlabeled data to reduce the JSD between two hypothesized misclassified classes. Our experimental results show that JSDMin? achieves superior or state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks and diverse poisoning settings, indicating its ability to counter a broad spectrum of attack methods. This can be accomplished by deploying optimized versions of these models known as pruned models. While models pruned using genetic algorithms have demonstrated excellent results, developing such models becomes challenging due to the high level of model sparsity created. This challenge poses difficulties in identifying model structures that can be efficiently utilized with inference accelerators. To address this challenge, we explore models pruned using recent advanced algorithms, such as amplitude-allocation algorithms, which result in a lower level of model sparsity. This approach allows us to design models in the form of dense networks, facilitating easier model acceleration. Our research focuses on applying these models to high-performance and resource-constrained deployments of Object Detection models, and we present novel, state-of-the-art models, such as PointRend gen and YOLOv3 gen, that excel at object detection tasks. We demonstrate that these models outperform their competing models in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and we also examine the potential for efficient inference acceleration, highlighting the ease of converting these models to integer formats for deployment on microcontrollers, a key step towards real-time, real-device object detection.

able Artificial Intelligence (XAI) poses a significant challenge in maintaining fidelity to the original model when explaining a target instance.  This occurs because the same model can produce vastly different explanations for that instance, which becomes crucial, particularly when employing machine learning in high-stakes applications such as healthcare.  It is made even more difficult when attempting to utilize the same method of explanation, which is necessary for a practical solution.  To address these difficulties, our work proposes an approach to generating differential privacy guarantees using the same explanation technique (feature selection based) for two contrasting deep neural network models trained on a dataset associated with a case of Alzheimer's disease classification.  In contrast to other methods, which either tailor the explanation to each individual model or sacrifice the use of a common explanation type, our method is able to leverage the same underlying technique, which is more aligned with real-world scenarios.  However, in the process, we discover that fidelity to the original model is compromised when trying to achieve differential privacy. and Fast R-CNN have gained widespread adoption in the field of object detection due to their high precision.  However, these methods rely on a pre-defined set of region proposals, which may not be adaptable to various applications that require real-time processing of novel objects.  To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel region proposal network (RPN) in collaboration with an improved version of R-CNN, which can learn directly from non-predefined training data sets.  The RPN we designed is a fully connected neural network that identifies the likelihood of each pixel belonging to a particular object class or background and predicts corresponding bounding box offsets.  The network's design allows for zero-shot detection of novel objects without the need for pre-defined candidate regions.  In collaboration with an enhanced R-CNN module, the novel RPN enables unsupervised and supervised learning of object detection directly from images that have no prior definition of object classes or background.  The improved R-CNN uses the candidate regions generated by the RPN to perform class-specific and background classification, along with precise class-specific object localization.  Our RPN design is versatile and can be utilized for both unsupervised and supervised learning setups.  The results of the novel single-image and large-scale benchmark experiments demonstrate that our RPN, in conjunction with our improved R-CNN, surpass the state-of-the-art results for single-image detection and rival top-performing proposal based methods on large-scale benchmarks. called WaveShaping to

The divergent part can be directly linked to the UV divergence in the Schwinger-Dyson equation for the electron's self-energy.  Specifically, we demonstrate that the UV divergence in the heat kernel expansion for the Dirac operator in six dimensions, which represents the self-energy problem, is responsible for the UV divergence in the one-loop effective action. To this end, we develop a unified framework that enables diverse uncertainty quantification strategies to be trained via delta-learning, a generic reinforcement learning method.  Our framework is framework-agnostic and can integrate prototypical deep learning, Bayesian neural networks, Bayesian optimization, variational UQ, and deep ensemble approaches.  Key features of our $\Delta$-UQ learning methodology include its ability to handle iterative and non-iterative uncertainty estimates via the application of reward functions and an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm.  Our study showcases the efficacy of this new method through comprehensive experiments and case studies, illustrating its utilization in diverse domains.

will play a crucial role in future space communications systems. To minimize costs and enhance efficiency in operating these systems, a single satellite test range is proposed for evaluating the communication links between earth stations and inter-satellite links (ISLs). Unlike previous studies that focused on Earth-to-Earth visibility, this research investigates visibility in a heterogeneous range consisting of different frequencies, wavelengths, satellite types, and communication angles. To achieve this, a Monte Carlo-based algorithm considering realistic orbital parameters and range constraints was developed and used to analyze the visibility of the ISLs. To further simplify range design, a statistical approach was adopted to determine the probability of range visibility. To validate the algorithm, it was applied to analyze a 13-satellite heterogeneous range, involving satellites from multiple major satellite constellations, and the results were visualized on 3D global maps. To facilitate efficient range operation, a genetic algorithm was proposed for automated range scheduling, taking into account the heterogeneous characteristics of the range, and demonstrated promising results in simulating 10 million opportunities to schedule one successful range communication.

Our primary interest lies in approximating the value function and optimal control policies for nonlinear systems, characterized by unbounded gradients and Hessian matrices.  We propose a Monte Carlo algorithm to solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation arising in stochastic control problems, effectively handling situations where the classical verification theorem is inapplicable.  Our method is grounded in a stochastic Taylor expansion that takes into account the impact of the Hessian matrix on the Bellman equation.  We illustrate the efficacy of our approach with several examples, including the calculation of the expected exit time from a domain, maximizing geometric Brownian motion, and minimizing stochastic differential equations with Gaussian measures.

a random word of a given size $n$ and length $m$ from a alphabet of size $d$ grows linearly with $m$ when $n$ is large, and linearly with $n$ when $m$ is large. The slope that indicates the rate of m's linear increase in the size of d's linear decrease is referred to as the entropy slope, and given by $ rac{1}{
u(d)}$, where $
u(d)$ is the word's entropy critical exponent and is defined for any finite alphabet. For a wide range of parameters $d$ and $m$, we investigate how the entropy slope is distributed across all words and identify four key factors that influence this distribution. Our findings show that the words' distribution of entropy slopes aligns with the distribution of their cluster counts and that the entropy slope is linked to the word's typical cluster structure. Moreover, we discover a direct entropy slope-diameter relationship for words with a diameter that is independent of both $n$ and $m$. In contrast, the diameter is directly proportional to $
u(d)$, and its independence from $m$ relies on $n$ being significantly larger than $m$. The findings are supported by theoretical analysis and extensive computer simulations.

Our analysis of the GRRM framework reveals a more practical and effective approach, Relative Minimax Risk Minimization (RelMMRM), which we prove equates to a form of max-min risk minimization.  We demonstrate that RelMMRM not only aligns with the theoretical underpinnings of RRM's success, yielding strong generalization guarantees, but also can be directly optimize with efficient solutions.  Our findings also reveal that RRM effectively integrates a form of entropy regularization into RelMMRM, explaining RRM's success and offering insights for improving other methods.  Our proofs show the equality of optimal RelMMRM solutions and the optimal GRRM solutions, highlighting the superiority of RelMMRM.  We also establish the smoothness properties of risk functions to enable efficient resolution of the RelMMRM problem.  Empirical evaluations show that our proposed Relative Minimax Risk Minimization (RelMMRM-Ada) algorithm outperforms the current top-performing method in experiments using the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet10.

approach to video super-resolution.  Our method leverages both inter and spatial correlations in videos to enhance the resolution of low-sampling-rate videos with high rates.  Specifically, we treat video super-resolution as an iterative high-rate to high-rate enhancement problem.  By applying approximate inverse operators, we aim to recover the original video frame from its down-sampled counterpart.  Due to the inherent ill-posed nature of this problem, we instead introduce a regularized optimization model that incorporates the implicit regularizer of consistent projections among enhanced down-sampled patches and original low-res patches.  The resulting model can be efficiently solved via our designed alternating direction algorithm.  Notably, the algorithm only requires solving implicit convolution operations.  Experimental evaluations on publicly available datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over other video super-resolution methods.  Moreover, our model exhibits remarkable potential for applications in real-time video processing.

We analyze the time required for the process to return to its starting state in a two-level subtree variant, and determine the distribution of this return time under specific conditions.  Additionally, we investigate the generator of the process in this restricted environment and utilize it to derive an expression for the transition rate. Weisstein demonstrated that certain elements in the homology of configuration spaces $H_*(conf_n(\mathbb{R}^2), \mathbb{Q})$ could not be accounted for by the homology of configuration spaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$, utilizing Poincaré duality and dimension arguments. Notably, this approach relies on properties unique to the configuration spaces in $\mathbb{R}3$ and may not be applicable in higher-dimensional spaces where duality is not a valid tool. This paper takes a different approach, centering on non-torsion elements in $H_*(conf_n(\mathbb{R}^2))$ that disappear in $H_*(conf_n(\mathbb{R}3))$. Specifically, polymers in such solvents encounter three primary effects: non-trivial attractive forces between monomers, temperature-dependent clumping, and entanglement among multiple polymers.  Our research employs both non-engaged and engaged polymers, modeled through Monte Carlo simulations, to analyze and compare their behavior in these three aspects.  
  In the presence of strong adhesive interactions, polymers become highly compact, making it possible to experiment with and observe their structural properties similar to those of dead polymers subjected to external pressure and without free-end movement.  Notably, the effective temperature at which simulated non-engaged polymers become compact is higher than that required for polymer exchange to occur, and these polymers demonstrate resistance to tangling upon heating, even after experiencing significant deformation due to heating.  
  Our results reveal that universal aspects of polymer behavior are consistent across non-engaged and engaged polymers, and the comparison of simulated results with theoretical predictions for random walks over lattice graphs with finite step sizes confirms an interesting correlation between effective and actual effective temperatures.  
  Our study holds practical implications for improving the accuracy of simulations used to model polymer exchange processes following annealing procedures, especially following the discovery of an unusual deformation caused by effective temperatures in these processes, which may also be applicable to annealing fused deposition modeling 3D-printed objects.

  e.g. EXR images, play a crucial role in computer graphics.  Unfortunately,
  traditional compression techniques fail to preserve the non-negative and
  piecewise smooth characteristics of environment maps while maintaining an
  acceptable file size and minimal loss of detail.  As a result, it's challenging
  to work with such maps in real-time applications, games, and visualizations.  Our
  approach, designed for these applications, aims to create compressed
  piecewise linear (PL) SCENARIO MAPS with a focus on preserving the characteristics
  of high dynamic range lighting while maintaining acceptable file sizes.  Our method
  achieves this by representing the environment map as a PL scenario map with a vertex
  count of around 12 using a custom loss function optimized via a penalty method
  and a penalty function solver based on an exterior point algorithm.  These compressed
  PL SCENARIO MAPS can be viewed using a standard QUAD VIEWER after being exported to an
  ODDITY MAP format, or applied in real-time applications such as THREE.JS by mapping
  them to a PL BUFFER.  Demonstration videos and example codes are available on our
  GitHub repository, along with an interactive website for interacting with the
  compressed PL SCENARIO MAPS.
